notes: Actual results for calendar year 2025, as the county reported them in its annual financial report to the Ohio Auditor of State (unaudited). Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included.

Governmental funds are reported by function. Capital outlay has no function, so it is spread over the other spending in proportion. Utility funds count operating revenue and expenses (depreciation left out) plus nonoperating revenue and debt payments.
Intergovernmental disbursements, payments to refunded bond escrow agents, borrowing, transfers, advances, sales of capital assets and special or extraordinary items are left out.
General government, courts, community and economic development and community environment count as overhead.
Debt is long-term obligations at year end (bonds, notes, loans and leases), as reported.
Political money is not scored: Ohio county candidates file campaign finance reports with their county board of elections, not with the state.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Ohio yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

notes: Actual results for calendar year 2025, as the township reported them in its annual financial report to the Ohio Auditor of State (unaudited). Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. Residents also pay Marion County.
A township serves the parts of it outside cities, and in most cases also the villages inside it.

Governmental funds are reported by function. Capital outlay has no function, so it is spread over the other spending in proportion. Utility funds count operating revenue and expenses (depreciation left out) plus nonoperating revenue and debt payments.
Intergovernmental disbursements, payments to refunded bond escrow agents, borrowing, transfers, advances, sales of capital assets and special or extraordinary items are left out.
General government, courts, community and economic development and community environment count as overhead.
Debt is long-term obligations at year end (bonds, notes, loans and leases), as reported.
Political money is not scored: Ohio local candidates file campaign finance reports with their county board of elections, not with the state.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 1 license-plate camera is mapped inside Prospect Township's borders in OpenStreetMap (1 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Ohio yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 1 Flock Safety license-plate camera is mapped inside Prospect Township's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.
